title: The Revival, the secrets of fasting
hookLine: three levels of fasting: the stomach, the limbs, the heart
tomorrow: if the heart is a mirror, what fogs it up?

lines: NO NEED OF HIS FOOD AND DRINK.
WHY WOULD A KEPT FAST BE UNNEEDED?
cards: Skipping lunch is easy, honestly. It happens by accident on a busy day. So what's the hard part of a fast?

Here's a strange line, kept in al-Bukhari, from the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Whoever does not give up false speech, and acting on it, God has no need of his giving up his food and drink. Read that twice.
Someone has gone hungry all day, from dawn to sunset, and the hadith says God has no need of it. Why would a fast that was kept be called unneeded?

teach.b: Al-Ghazali answers in the Revival, in his book on the secrets of fasting, by describing three levels. The first is the fast of the stomach: no food, no drink, no intimacy from dawn to sunset.
It's real, and it's required in Ramadan.
The second is the fast of the limbs: the eyes kept from what harms, the ears from gossip, the tongue from lies and cruelty, the hands and feet from wrong.
The third is the fast of the heart: holding the heart back from everything but God. Now the puzzle comes apart. The hadith isn't saying the hunger is worthless.
It's saying the hunger was meant to carry something. A stomach that fasts while the tongue keeps lying has kept the outside and missed the point.
In another hadith in al-Bukhari, if someone picks a fight with a fasting person, they're told to say simply: I am fasting.
The fast reaches the mouth before the food does. And here's a line worth knowing, from the Qur'an itself: "Fasting is prescribed for you, even as it was prescribed for those before you."
Fasting, the Qur'an says, didn't begin with Muslims. What al-Ghazali adds is the depth: the stomach is the door, not the whole house.

how: Muslims fast from dawn to sunset in Ramadan and some voluntarily on other days; some teachers add al-Ghazali's reminder to fast with the eyes, ears and tongue as well.

games.q: the three fasts — tap the pairs.
p: no food or drink, dawn to sunset
eyes, ears, tongue kept from harm

s: the hadith says hunger during a fast is worthless
it says the hunger was meant to carry something: a fast that keeps lying has missed the point.
the Qur'an says fasting was prescribed for those before Muslims too
"even as it was prescribed for those before you" (2:183).
for al-Ghazali, the fast of the stomach doesn't matter
it's real and required in Ramadan. it's the door, not the whole house.

games.q: you're fasting, and at practice a teammate makes a cutting joke about you in front of everyone. you've got the perfect comeback. what fits the hadith?
o: fire it back; the fast is about food, not words.
say it, then make it up to them after sunset.
let it go and say: I am fasting.
games.why: in al-Bukhari, a fasting person who's provoked is told to say simply: I am fasting. the fast reaches the tongue before the food.

practice: Rest your eyes on one plain object near you: a cup, a doorframe, your own hand. Keep them there for the whole sit, and let your eyes fast from everything else. When they wander, bring them back without scolding.

wordCard.voice: The Revival, again: here its book on fasting, with three levels, the stomach, the limbs and the heart.

orig.note: Arabic: sawm, fasting; al-Ghazali describes three levels of it.

carryVoice: Carry this: the fast of the heart, where the hunger was always pointing. Five days into al-Ghazali.
